title: Should in that-clauses; the present subjunctive

sections.title: Should in that-clauses
sections.content:
We can sometimes report advice, orders, requests, suggestions, etc. about things that need to be done or are desirable using a that-clause with should + bare infinitive:
• They have proposed that Felix should move to their Munich office.
• We advised that the company should not raise its prices.
After should we often use be + past participle (passive) or be + adjective:
• They directed that the building should be pulled down.
• We insist that the money should be available to all students in financial difficulties.

sections.title: The present subjunctive
sections.content:
In formal contexts, particularly in written English, we can often leave out should and use only the bare infinitive. This form is the present subjunctive and is used to describe bringing about the situation expressed in the that-clause:
• They have proposed that Felix move to their Munich office.
• They directed that the building be pulled down.
Other verbs used with the present subjunctive: advise, ask, beg, command, demand, insist, instruct, intend, order, prefer, recommend, request, require, stipulate, suggest, urge, warn.
To make a negative form, we use not (without 'do') before the verb:
• We advised that the company not raise its prices.
In less formal contexts we can use ordinary forms of the verb instead of the subjunctive. Compare:
• I suggested that he should give up golf. (negative: ... that he shouldn't give up ...)
• I suggested that he give up golf. (more formal) (negative: ... that he not give up ...)
• I suggested that he gives up golf. (less formal) (negative: ... that he doesn't give up ...)

sections.title: With nouns and adjectives
sections.content:
We can also use that-clauses with should or the subjunctive after reporting clauses with nouns related to the verbs in B (e.g. advice, order, proposal, warning):
• The police issued an order that all weapons (should) be handed in immediately.
We can also use that-clauses with should or the subjunctive after adjectives such as advisable, crucial, desirable, essential, imperative, important, necessary, vital:
• It is essential that she (should) have a medical examination.

exercises.question: Lee felt that business in South America ___ ___ (expand - passive).
exercises.hint: Passive form after 'should': be + past participle.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should be expanded
Passive form after 'should': be + past participle. Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.

exercises.sentence: The doctor recommended that she takes complete rest for a week.
exercises.correction: The doctor recommended that she take complete rest for a week.
acceptable: that she should take complete rest
exercises.hint: After verbs of recommendation/demand, use the bare subjunctive (no -s) or 'should + infinitive'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: that she take complete rest
After verbs of recommendation, demand, and suggestion (recommend, suggest, insist, demand, require, propose, request, urge), the that-clause uses either: (1) the bare subjunctive: 'that she take' (no -s even for third person) or (2) 'should + infinitive': 'that she should take'. Both are correct.

exercises.question: It would be valuable for us to send a sales representative to South Africa. -> Alice recommended that a sales representative ___ to South Africa.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: (should) be sent
Passive subjunctive: be + past participle. Choose the passive form that matches the tense and aspect of the active version.

exercises.sentence: It is essential that he is present at the board meeting.
exercises.correction: It is essential that he be present at the board meeting.
exercises.hint: After 'it is essential/vital/crucial/important that', use the bare subjunctive 'be' not 'is'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: that he be present
Adjective constructions expressing necessity (essential, vital, crucial, important, necessary, imperative + that) trigger the subjunctive. Use the bare form 'be' for all persons: 'that he be', 'that she be', 'that they be'. 'That he should be' is also correct and is common in British English.

exercises.question: Look at this sentence: 'Lee felt that business in South America should be expanded.' Can it be written without 'should' (subjunctive)?
exercises.hint: With 'feel' we don't usually use the subjunctive.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: No
The subjunctive is triggered by verbs of recommendation/demand/necessity (suggest, insist, recommend, require). 'Feel' does not trigger the subjunctive — use an indicative that-clause or a to-infinitive instead.

exercises.sentence: The committee proposed that the funding should allocated equally.
exercises.correction: The committee proposed that the funding should be allocated equally.
exercises.hint: Passive + subjunctive: should be + past participle (missing 'be').
exercises.explanation:
Answer: should be allocated equally
In passive subjunctive constructions: should + be + past participle. 'Should allocated' is missing the auxiliary 'be'. The full passive structure must be: should + be + past participle. Compare active: 'that they allocate equally' vs passive: 'that it should be allocated equally'.

exercises.question: It is ___ / she / marry Ben. (Select the most appropriate adjective for a strong recommendation/necessity).
options: inconceivable that she should marry Ben.
amused that she should marry Ben.
upset that she should marry Ben.
shocked that she should marry Ben.
exercises.hint: Inconceivable fits the structural prompt well.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: inconceivable that she should marry Ben.
Inconceivable fits the structural prompt well.

exercises.question: I am ___ / Kristina / behave so badly. (Select adj expressing emotional reaction).
options: shocked that Kristina should behave so badly.
imperative that Kristina should behave so badly.
urgent that Kristina should behave so badly.
vital that Kristina should behave so badly.
exercises.hint: 'Shocked' expresses an emotional reaction to a fact, followed by a should-clause.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: shocked that Kristina should behave so badly.
'Shocked' expresses an emotional reaction to a fact, followed by a should-clause. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.
